item.content:encoded:
Major League Baseball’s playoffs are coming soon and Alex Bregman will be a part of it.
Of course he is.
Bregman made baseball history Thursday, Sept. 24 when the Chicago Cubs clinched a National League wild-card berth with a victory over the Miami Marlins. And for the 10th consecutive year, injured eye willing, Bregman will take part in the postseason, this time with a twist.
Bregman, the Cubs’ 32-year-old third baseman, will become the first position player to play postseason baseball 10 consecutive seasons with multiple teams. In fact, he’s done it with three ballclubs – eight straight years with the Houston Astros and then the past two with the Boston Red Sox and Cubs, as he settled for good in Chicago by signing a five-year, $175 million contract in January.
And it seems like wherever Bregman goes, October baseball follows.
Texas loves him anyway
Bregman was a two-time All-Star and two-time champion in Houston, the brash young slugger in his first full season when they won the 2017 World Series, the MVP runner-up when they lost the 2019 Series in seven games.
After bearing much of the scorn for the club’s 2017 sign-stealing scandal, he was the chastened veteran on the 2022 squad that won a second World Series, this time without a cloud of controversy to follow.
Yet Bregman’s chops as a club cornerstone gained greater veracity a year ago, when he left the Astros and, combining his production with his baseball smarts and clubhouse gravitas, lifted the Red Sox to the postseason for the first time in three years as the Astros missed the playoffs for the first time since 2016.
Those vibes were as attractive to the Cubs as Bregman’s career .846 OPS when they pursued him after he opted out of his contract with Boston. And it’s all come together in Wrigleyville: Thanks to a second-half surge, Bregman has hit 26 home runs, posted an .804 OPS and produced 5.4 WAR, second only to presumed MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong on the Cubs.
“Anytime Alex Bregman is playing an Alex Bregman brand of baseball, it’s just good for the program,” Crow-Armstrong told USA TODAY Sports last month.
And if he manages to play just days after suffering a gruesome eye injury, the legend will only grow.
Heroes of the fall
Bregman’s postseason constancy has put himself among some legendary and curious October stalwarts.
Advertisement
Unsurprisingly, the consecutive postseasons list is littered with alumni from the three dominant playoff groups of the wild-card era: The 1990s Atlanta Braves, the late-century New York Yankees and the current batch of Los Angeles Dodgers.
Yankees closer Mariano Rivera tops the list, appearing in 13 consecutive postseasons from 1995-2007, followed by Derek Jeter, whose 12-year streak began a year after Rivera’s playoff debut.
Catcher Jorge Posada and Braves Hall of Famers Chipper Jones and Tom Glavine all played in 11 consecutive postseasons. As did lefty reliever Mike Stanton, who did it with four teams – the Braves, Red Sox, Yankees and Texas Rangers – between 1991-2002.
Who let him in?
Bregman, longtime Dodgers closer Kenley Jansen and Hall of Famer Greg Maddux all reached 10 consecutive postseasons. Current Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman and longtime third baseman Justin Turner are at the nine-year mark, Freddie winning a World Series championship with Atlanta in 2021 and two more in L.A. the past two seasons.
Retired Dodgers lefty Clayton Kershaw leads the “but for” category: He pitched in eight consecutive postseasons from 2013-2020, and would have made it 13 in a row if not for injuries in 2021 and 2024. Same with Braves Hall of Famer John Smoltz – he was present for all of Atlanta’s 14 consecutive division titles yet underwent Tommy John surgery in 2000.
And several likely 2026 participants had streaks broken thanks to one unlucky season – such as slugger Kyle Schwarber, who’d be working on a 12-year streak with the Cubs, Red Sox and Phillies if not for the 2019 Cubs missing the playoffs. Same with Mookie Betts, ticketed for his 10th postseason in 11 years with the Dodgers and Boston, missing only in ’19 with the Red Sox.
The wild-card format – which began in 1995 and expanded in 2012 and 2022 – makes this list unavoidably modern due to the expanded access it affords. Still, some players from past eras were near-constants in the playoffs.
Mr. October himself, Reggie Jackson, reached the postseason 10 times in 12 years from 1971 to 1982, winning four World Series with the Oakland Athletics and New York Yankees, and then, just for kicks, reaching the 1982 ALCS with the California Angels.
The great Yogi Berra was a 10-time World Series champion, but his longest consecutive streak of playoff runs was five years. Yet reaching the World Series 14 times in 17 years, when only two teams reached the playoffs, remains a stunning feat.
So perhaps Bregman - even with 102 career postseason games, 19 homers, 91 hits and a .791 OPS - has a little more work to do to match some of the legends of October. Yet from Houston to Boston to Chicago, he’s leaving little doubt that wherever he goes, winning follows.
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Alex Bregman's wild MLB playoff streak has star in rare air – injured face willing

item.title: [mlb.com] Hall of Fame broadcaster Matthews to be celebrated for 8,000th game of legendary career

item.content:encoded:
KANSAS CITY -- On a cold winter day during this past offseason, a dozen Royals media members gathered in the Kauffman Stadium press box to go through decades of baseball history.
Every single game Hall of Fame broadcaster Denny Matthews has ever called -- starting from the first Royals game in 1969 -- has been preserved through his scorecards, sorted by year, then eventually decade, and separated in manilla folders. Stars from the past fill these lineup cards -- Nolan Ryan, George Brett, Reggie Jackson, Cal Ripken Jr., Rickey Henderson, Ken Griffey Jr. among them -- telling the stories of thousands of games that Matthews has called throughout his legendary baseball career.
A few of those scorecards detail some of the Royals’ most iconic moments, like Kansas City’s two World Series titles or Brett’s 3,000th hit, signed by the Hall of Famer himself, but others are another day at the ballpark -- a single day in one of the 58 years and counting of Royals baseball.
Matthews has been in the booth for every single one. And after counting 86.6% of the total possible scorebooks in Royals history, it was discovered that Matthews will be calling his 8,000th game on Friday night against the Guardians at Kauffman Stadium.
"I don’t think I’ve really accepted that yet. It’s still just a number, and maybe when the season is over and I start thinking about that, it’ll take on a little different tone," Matthews said. "But that’s a lot of foul balls."
Matthews will be honored for his one-of-a-kind career on the television broadcast, as well as a special moment on the field, during Friday’s game in recognition of the achievement. But don’t worry, Matthews is planning to return for his 59th season in 2027.
“There’s so many reasons why I am still in Kansas City and the biggest reason is, I’m going to say organization but that doesn’t mean a lot, because organizations are people. And the reason that I’ve been around this long is because of the people I’ve associated with,” Matthews said.
“It’s the people that count. All in all, that’s why I’m still sitting here instead of being in Chicago or St. Louis -- or Cucamonga.”
That one-liner is a perfect example of the quick wit and humor listeners have come to expect from the longtime broadcaster. But he’s also telling the truth, at least about the first two cities. Matthews grew up in Illinois, between St. Louis and Chicago, and had dreamed as a young broadcaster of eventually moving on to cover one of the teams who he grew up listening to.
When Matthews was 10 years old, he would lay in front of the radio and listen to broadcasters such as Jack Buck and Jack Brickhouse, taking in their every word and falling in love with the game. Like every kid, his real dream was to play, of course, and Matthews did in high school and college before turning to broadcasting -- although he wouldn’t cover baseball until the Royals.
“Listening to those guys, all those summer nights, I was getting a great college education in how to broadcast baseball, and I didn’t have to pay any tuition and I didn’t have to do homework,” Matthews said. “... A lot of that was in my mind when I probably sat down and would describe a play the way that Jack Buck or Jack Brickhouse did. But when I was hearing all those games all those years and it was preparing me, I had no idea what I was eventually [going to do]. That’s pretty cool I think.”
Buddy Blattner and Matthews formed the first Royals radio broadcast duo in club history in 1969, and it was Blattner that helped guide the then-26-year-old Matthews while he settled into the booth and began forming his signature broadcasting style.
“One thing that is really underappreciated about him is not just his ability to describe the game, but his ability to analyze the game,” said broadcaster Ryan Lefebvre, who has worked with Matthews since 1999. “... He has a great feel for the game, which sets him up to see things happen before they actually happen. And it’s not like he has this crystal ball and ability to look into the future, … but I’ve been with him in the booth when he’s predicted things a pitch or two before they happen, and it’s just amazing.
“The feel for the game that he has and his ability to analyze the game hasn’t been part of describing Denny Matthews as much as it should be.”
It wasn’t long before other teams noticed that talent, including large markets like Chicago and New York, but a conversation with Royals founder and former owner Ewing Kauffman left a lasting impression on Matthews after just his third season in the booth.
“[Kauffman] said, ‘I’ll tell you what young man. You’re going to have other opportunities and decisions to make … but I want to tell you one thing, we like the way you do the games and you can stay here as long as you want,’” Matthews said. “... So here we are, 58 years later.
“The Kansas City Royals to me have been family.”
Matthews has in turn been a central part of baseball families in Kansas City, spanning generations of Royals fans as a common voice. He’s just one of four announcers in MLB history to broadcast for the same team for at least 50 seasons, joining Vin Scully (67 with Dodgers), Jaime Jarrín (64 with Dodgers) and Bob Uecker (54 with Brewers).
Matthews called 99.5% of Royals games from 1969-2000, missing only 23 games over 32 seasons (5,061 out of 5,084). He’s been calling games since before Apollo 11 landed on the moon, and even when it did, Matthews called both games of a doubleheader against the White Sox at Comiskey Park on July 20, 1969.
He’s watched the introduction of the designated hitter (1973), the Wild Card (1995), Interleague Play (1997), pitch clock (2023) and much more while providing a stable voice in the booth while the sport and world changed around him for nearly six decades. Matthews has called games featuring the franchises oldest-born (Ted Abernathy, 1933) and youngest-born player (Carter Jensen, 2003) in club history. Matthews even got married last year inside Kauffman Stadium.
“He is a walking, living, breathing encyclopedia of the Kansas City Royals,” Lefebvre said. “There is nobody that comes close as far as being able to, not just know the history of the Royals, but have observed the history of the Royals. … It’s kind of like sitting at the feet of your grandfather and just learning from someone who has experienced so much life. And to be able to turn words into pictures, and turn pictures into words, there’s nobody else in Major League Baseball like him.”
Matthews was inducted into Cooperstown in 2007 following his Royals Hall of Fame induction in 2004. He’s a Ford C. Frick Award winner, one of the highest honors for a broadcaster, and is in the Missouri Sports Hall of Fame.
And he’s still sitting in the Royals broadcast booth in 2026, calling every home game. His road trips have declined in recent years, although he makes occasional appearances at Busch Stadium and Wrigley Field, but his love for the game hasn’t. He returned to Spring Training this season after not traveling to Arizona the past couple of years because in his words, “I missed it.”
Radios across Kansas City have broadcast the words of Matthews for decades during Royals games. It’s been that way literally forever. And on Friday night that impact will be celebrated.
“Denny has always been there. Denny is the constant of Royals baseball,” said broadcaster Jake Eisenberg. “The very first time that they played a game, Denny’s the one who said, ‘Royals win.’ When they win their next game, he’ll be the one that says, ‘Royals win.’
“There is nobody like Denny Matthews that has existed in baseball history, and there is nobody that ever will again. There is nobody that has been the voice of a franchise, since its existence, for as long as he has been … and we should not take that for granted.”

item.title: [MLB.com] ¡De locura! Dieciséis datos asombrosos de la temporada del 2026
item.dc:creator: Anthony Castrovince
item.description: En el Día Inaugural de este año, los Cardenales y Rays jugaron un partido en el que cada uno anotó seis carreras o más en la sexta entrada. Apenas llevábamos unas horas en la temporada del 2026, y ya los investigadores del Elias Sports Bureau estaban buscando en los libros de récords para encontrar que un juego del 19 de abril de 1890 entre los Boston Beaneaters y los Brooklyn Bridegrooms marcó la última vez que dos escuadras habían anotado tantas rayitas en un solo inning en un partido inaugura
item.content:encoded:
En el Día Inaugural de este año, los Cardenales y Rays jugaron un partido en el que cada uno anotó seis carreras o más en la sexta entrada. Apenas llevábamos unas horas en la temporada del 2026, y ya los investigadores del Elias Sports Bureau estaban buscando en los libros de récords para encontrar que un juego del 19 de abril de 1890 entre los Boston Beaneaters y los Brooklyn Bridegrooms marcó la última vez que dos escuadras habían anotado tantas rayitas en un solo inning en un partido inaugural.
Así comenzó nuestra dosis diaria de estadísticas de locura en el béisbol.
Ahora que la campaña del 2026 está a punto de terminar, revisemos esos libros para ver cuáles números extraños de todo el año la han hecho tan especial.
(Todas las estadísticas son hasta los juegos del martes. Como de costumbre, ¡gracias a la investigadora Sarah Langs, que es increíble en el mejor de los sentidos, por su ayuda en la recopilación de esta lista!)
.673
El OPS de Pete Crow-Armstrong al llegar al primer tercio de la temporada de los Cachorros. Esto, de un muchacho que terminó registrando una temporada de 10 de fWAR (la versión de FanGraphs de Victorias por Encima del Reemplazo) y que probablemente se lleve fácilmente el premio a Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Nacional.
Nunca ha habido un giro similar. Entre los 56 jugadores anteriores en tener una campaña de 10 de fWAR, éstas fueron las marcas de OPS más bajas en el primer tercio:
Eddie Collins, Atléticos de Filadelfia de 1909: .826
Mike Trout, Angelinos del 2012: .835
Honus Wagner, Piratas de 1908: .894
Trout, Angelinos del 2013: .920
Wagner, Piratas de 1905: .924
Como pueden ver, nadie se había acercado a un OPS tan bajo como el de PCA en el primer tercio de la campaña de camino a un total de WAR tan extraordinario. PCA sólo valía 1.4 de fWAR en ese momento. Ahora, podemos decir que ha tenido posiblemente la mejor temporada individual en la historia de la no tan joven franquicia de los Cachorros. Un repunte en plena campaña para el recuerdo.
200+
Tanto Jacob Misiorowski de los Cerveceros (223) como Cam Schlittler de los Yankees (217) tienen EFE+ por encima de 200, lo que significa que han sido más del doble de buenos que el promedio de la liga. Por eso son los presuntos favoritos para los Premios Cy Young.
En primer lugar, es inusual contar con dos lanzadores con una EFE+ de al menos 200 en una sola campaña. Eso sólo ha ocurrido dos veces en una temporada completa en este siglo: En el 2015 (Jake Arrieta y Zack Greinke) y en el 2018 (Jacob deGrom y Blake Snell).
Pero lo doblemente asombroso aquí es que tanto Misiorowski como Schlittler están apenas en su segunda campaña en las Mayores. Los únicos otros monticulares en la Era de la Bola Viva (desde 1920) en tener una EFE+ de al menos 200 en su primera o segunda temporada fueron Dwight Gooden en su legendaria campaña de 1985 (229) y Paul Skenes en su año del Cy Young en el 2025 (226).
81
Victorias para los Medias Blancas. Eso es por mucho la mayor cantidad para un equipo después de tres temporadas consecutivas de 100 derrotas o más. El récord anterior había sido de 70, logrado por los Astros del 2014, los Senadores de Washington de 1965 y los Bravos de Boston de 1925.
Ningún equipo ha clasificado para los playoffs después de siquiera dos campañas seguidas de 100 derrotas. Los Patipálidos podrían convertirse en los primeros.
106
Bases por bolas para el cañonero cubano de los Astros, Yordan Álvarez -- la mayor cantidad en las Mayores.
Si Álvarez de alguna manera puede conseguir la Triple Corona de la Liga Americana en estos días finales (necesita superar a Pete Alonso por el título de impulsadas), no sólo sería el primero en lograr esa hazaña en cualquiera de las ligas desde el venezolano Miguel Cabrera en el 2012. También sería apenas el segundo jugador en ganar una Triple Corona y a la vez liderar la liga en bases por bolas. Ted Williams lo hizo en 1942 y 1947.
Para los niños que nos leen: Ustedes quieren batear como Ted Williams. Eso es algo bueno.
16
El número de jugadores esta temporada que han dado jonrón en su debut en MLB. Es un nuevo récord, tres más que el tope anterior establecido en el 2022.
2
Salvamentos para el as dominicano de los Marlins, Sandy Alcántara, quien además es el líder en entradas lanzadas en las Grandes Ligas (213.0). Desde que el rescate se convirtió en una estadística oficial en 1969, la única vez, según Elias, que un lanzador registró un salvamento en una campaña en la que lideró Grandes Ligas en entradas lanzadas fue cuando Phil Niekro lo hizo en 1978.
2
El número de equipos para los cuales Jo Adell ha conectado el cuadrangular más largo de la campaña. Dio un bambinazo de 449 pies para los Angelinos el 10 de mayo y luego, tras un cambio a mitad de año, conectó uno de 455 pies para los Guardianes el 18 de agosto. Ningún otro jugador en la Era Statcast ha dado el vuelacercas más largo de su club en múltiples equipos en la misma temporada.
3.98
La proporción de ponches por cada base por bolas del novato de los Guardianes, Parker Messick. Messick podría ser finalista al Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, gracias a un comando que es sumamente inusual para alguien con tan poca experiencia en Grandes Ligas. El único otro novato en la Era Moderna (desde 1900) con al menos 180 entradas y una mejor proporción K/BB fue el miembro del Salón de la Fama Don Sutton (4.02), con los Dodgers de 1966.
6.7
El bWAR (modelo de Victorias Sobre Reemplazo de Baseball-Reference) de la sensación novata de los Tigres, Kevin McGonigle. Es el más alto de todos los tiempos para un jugador en una temporada de debut en la que pasó la mayor parte del año con 21 años o menos. La marca anterior era de 6.6, conseguida tres veces: Por el dominicano Albert Pujols en el 2001, Frank Robinson en 1956 y aquel tal Ted Williams que mencionamos anteriormente, en 1939.
1.16
La efectividad de Cam Schlittler como visitante. Es la tercera mejor en la Era de la Pelota Viva para un lanzador con al menos 100 episodios fuera de casa. Las únicas mejores cifras pertenecieron a los miembros del Salón de la Fama Bob Gibson (0.81) en 1968 y Greg Maddux (1.12) en 1995. (Cabe destacar que ninguno estaba en su segunda temporada de Grandes Ligas en ese momento).
235
El EFE+ de Shohei Ohtani en 85.2 innings lanzados.
Es demasiado fácil acostumbrarse a lo que hace Ohtani e incluso restarle importancia a su campaña como jugador de dos vías, dado que los problemas de lesiones lo obligaron a dejar de lanzar a principios de julio. ¡Pero esto no es normal! En la Era Moderna, apenas otros ocho abridores de las Ligas Americana/Liga Nacional han registrado un EFE+ de al menos ese nivel con un mínimo de 85 entradas lanzadas:
Jacob deGrom, Mets de 2021: 373
Pedro Martínez, Medias Rojas de 2000: 291
Greg Maddux, Bravos de 1994: 271
Maddux, Bravos de 1995: 260
Bob Gibson, Cardenales de 1968: 258
Clayton Kershaw, Dodgers de 2016: 237
Clay Buchholz, Medias Rojas de 2013: 237
Obviamente, es inherentemente más impresionante registrar un EFE+ de ese nivel lanzando durante una temporada más completa. ¿Pero saben qué más es impresionante? Conseguir un EFE+ tan alto mientras también registras OPS de .902 en casi 600 visitas al plato.
De nuevo, no es normal. Ni siquiera para Ohtani.
47
La cifra de bases robadas, líder de las Mayores, del segunda base de los Nacionales, el dominicano Nasim Núñez, quien por lo demás está teniendo dificultades ofensivas esta temporada. Núñez tiene OPS de .529. El único otro jugador en la Era Moderna con OPS inferior a .550 que aun así logró robarse 40 bases fue Rollie Zeider (OPS de .548, 49 robos) de los Medias Blancas de 1910.
.374
El porcentaje de slugging de Cal Raleigh. El mismo Cal Raleigh que disparó 60 cuadrangulares la temporada pasada. De las nueve ocasiones anteriores en las que un jugador tuvo una campaña de 60 bambinazos, el porcentaje de slugging más bajo en la campaña siguiente había sido el .485 de Roger Maris en 1962. Eso sigue siendo más de 100 puntos superior al de Raleigh, quien pasó de ocupar el tercer lugar entre los bateadores calificados de MLB en SLG el año pasado (.589) a estar ahora entre los últimos 25.
42
Salvamentos desperdiciados por los Nacionales, un nuevo récord de Grandes Ligas. La marca anterior era de 36, establecida por los Medias Blancas en el 2024, cuando perdieron 121 juegos. Se podría decir que los Nacionales hicieron “volar” ese récord.
217, 28
Totales de ponches de los compañeros de los Filis Kyle Schwarber y el venezolano Luis Arráez, respectivamente. Schwarber está compitiendo por el liderato de ponches de MLB, mientras que Arráez (quien llegó procedente de los Gigantes en un cambio durante la Fecha Límite) terminará de último en ponches entre los bateadores calificados de la Gran Carpa.
Según Elias, sólo ha habido cuatro ocasiones en la Era de la Expansión (desde 1961) en las que el líder de MLB en ponches y el jugador con la menor cantidad de ponches (nuevamente, entre los bateadores calificados) terminaron la campaña en el mismo equipo… ¡y dos de ellas también involucraron a los Filis!
Medias Blancas de 1963: Dave Nicholson (más ponches), Nellie Fox (menos ponches)
Filis de 1965: Dick Allen (más), Octavio “Cookie” Rojas (menos)
Filis de 1976: Mike Schmidt (más), Dave Cash (menos)
Angelinos de 1982: Reggie Jackson (más), Tim Foli (menos)
0.8
Terminemos con la recta. Éste es el porcentaje de todos los pitcheos en MLB este año que han sido registrados a 100 mph o más. No se trata sólo de que sea el porcentaje más alto de la era de seguimiento de pitcheos (que se remonta al 2008), sino de que ni siquiera está cerca. ¡La cantidad de pitcheos de 100 mph o más ha aumentado en un 43.5%… tan sólo desde el año pasado!
Una razón más para que tengan nuestro permiso de ignorar a cualquier veterano que intente decirles que antes los lanzadores tiraban igual de duro.

item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice is in the process of wrapping up a breakout season for the New York Yankees. That included making some history on Wednesday.
Facing the Tampa Bay Rays, the All-Star first baseman opened the scoring in the first inning with his 40th homer of the season. It was a second-deck no-doubter off a first-pitche sinker from Rays starter Mason Englert.
Then he hit another in the fourth inning, putting him in a four-way tie for the AL lead at 41 homers with Pete Alonso, Yordan Álvarez and Junior Caminero.
By reaching 40 homers in a season, Rice has entered rare territory. As MLB.com's Sarah Langs notes, he joins teammate Aaron Judge as the second Yankees draft pick to post a 40-homer season.
Yes, only the second.
Obviously, the Yankees have more than fair share of elite sluggers in history. It's just that many of the homegrown ones entered the league before 1965, when the MLB Draft was first instituted. Others began their careers with other teams before joining the Yankees.
Here is the complete list of Yankees players to post a 40-homer season and how they joined New York, with pre-draft players italicized:
- Aaron Judge (draft pick)
- Roger Maris (trade)
- Mickey Mantle (signed)
- Lou Gehrig (signed)
- Joe DiMaggio (signed)
- Tino Martinez (trade)
- Reggie Jackson (free agent)
- Ben Rice (draft pick)
There are other Yankees draft picks who have come close, with Fred McGriff, Steve Balboni and Don Mattingly all posting a season with at least 35 homers.
McGriff, a ninth-round Yankees pick in 1981, came closest to 40 among that group with 37 in a 1993 season split between the Atlanta Braves and San Diego Padres. He never played a game for New York, having been traded as minor leaguer in a now-infamous deal for Dale Murray and Tom Dodd.
As for some other famous names, Derek Jeter never hit more than 24 and Bernie Williams never hit more than 30.
It's all a fun little quirk of history, created by the flow of both the Yankees and the MLB rulebook through the time. It actually requires quite a lot to go right for a draft pick to hit 40 homers in even a single season.
